This Afternoon - Friday Morning: Strong/Severe Storm and Heavy 
Rain Potential 

A messy scenario continues across the region as ongoing showers
and storms through much of the morning have been able to linger
into this afternoon, and have really put a damper on the 
atmosphere's ability to recover and destabilize as we head into 
the evening and overnight hours. An area of storms has developed
across eastern North Dakota this afternoon associated with a 
shortwave trough ejecting off the longwave trough across the 
Pacific Northwest. This area of storms is expected to grow 
upscale into an MCS through the afternoon before translating 
east-southeastward across Minnesota into northern Wisconsin this
evening and overnight. 

There are a couple different scenarios in the CAMs as far as 
how this potential propagates is concerned. Many model solutions
suggest the MCS makes it into our northern tier of counties, 
mainly along and north of I-94 though possibly as far south as 
I-90 in Wisconsin. Other solutions suggest that it stays north 
of our area, closer to the Wisconsin/Upper Michigan border. What
track it ultimately takes is a bit uncertain, but would tend 
towards more of a southern solution given the expected placement
of a northward advancing warm front. However, because of the 
lingering showers and storms early this afternoon, the 03.15z 
RAP depicts a weakening MUCAPE gradient with southeastward 
extent from North Dakota into northern Wisconsin. This would 
suggest that if the MCS is able to maintain itself across 
Minnesota, it would tend to weaken as it approaches our area. 

From a strong to severe standpoint, the greatest threat area
would be along and north of I-90 and across Wisconsin where the 
MUCAPE gradient and effective shear is maximized. Would expect 
damaging wind gusts to be the main hazard given the linear mode 
and DCAPE values of 900-1000 J/kg though can't rule out an 
isolated tornado if the system becomes surface based (an 
unlikely scenario) given sufficient low level turning depicted 
in model hodographs and 0-3km shear values of 30-35kts. That 
said, it currently looks as though the bulk of any severe 
convection would occur to our northwest or southeast, especially
if it tends to weaken as it moves into Wisconsin. 

Even if stronger to severe convection is not able to sustain 
itself into our area, fairly efficient rain rates and heavy 
rainfall are a concern overnight given the west-east oriented 
boundary across the region with the aforementioned strengthening
low level jet and moisture transport axis across the region. 
Conditions are ripe for heavy rainfall with PWATs over 1.5 
inches and warm cloud depths of 10kft or greater. This heavy 
rainfall is most likely across western into central Wisconsin 
where storms are most favorable to frequent, though this 
potential is on the lower side (10-20%). Regardless, rainfall 
amounts in the 25th-75th percentiles of the 03.12z HREF are 
around 0.5-1.75 inches, respectively, although the potential for
localized areas of 3 inches or more exists per the LPMM.

Friday Afternoon: Additional Storm Potential, Low Severe Chance

Mid to upper level ridging begins building across the central 
United States Friday but not before a shortwave trough is able 
to translate eastward into the Upper Midwest. Some model 
solutions suggest the quasi-stationary warm front shifts back 
southward Friday morning behind the MCS associated with its 
outflow boundary, stalling again somewhere around to just south 
of I-90. Forcing is expected to be weak while low level capping 
remains in place, so where or even if convection is able to 
initiate Friday afternoon will likely be dependent on how 
storms evolve tonight.

Assuming storms are able to develop, some stronger updrafts are
possible given MLCAPE values of 2500-3500 J/kg which would 
support some hail development and some stronger wind gusts given
DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. However effective shear will 
be meager, around 20kts, so updrafts that do develop will be 
unlikely to sustain themselves.

Outside of the storm potential, high temperatures reach around
90 degrees across northeast Iowa into southwest Wisconsin 
Friday afternoon. With the humid airmass remaining in place 
across the region, heat indices may approach 100 degrees during 
the afternoon hours, mainly for those along and south of 
Highway 18.
